references.name: Donald Hoffman
references.tldr: American cognitive scientist who argues that evolution shaped our senses to hide reality rather than reveal it. He goes further and proposes that space, time and matter are not fundamental; networks of 'conscious agents' are, and physics should be derived from them.
references.bach_take: Bach accepts the first half (the world looks nothing like our experience of it) and rejects the second: he thinks Hoffman misunderstands what a computer is and told him in the debate that he was 'outing himself' as a mysterian.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I buy Donald Hoffman's first part of the theory, which is typically, the world looks nothing like what we experience it as.
It's interesting that you start outing yourself as a mysterionist in a way, right?

references.name: Interface theory of perception and conscious agents
references.author: Donald Hoffman
references.tldr: Hoffman's claim that perception works like a desktop interface: icons tuned for survival, not truth ('fitness beats truth'). His companion theory models reality as interacting conscious agents described by Markov kernels, with spacetime as a derived data structure.
references.bach_take: Bach agrees that perception is a constructed model but stays with computationalism: brains differ from PCs, yet are still describable as Turing machines, so there is no need to make consciousness the base layer.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Hoffman: 'These conscious agents in the mathematics, they get certain inputs. We can call them experiences that they have.' (Hoffman speaking; Bach debates this framework for the whole episode)
But this doesn't mean that they cannot be described as Turing machines.

references.name: John Vervaeke
references.tldr: Toronto cognitive scientist known for the lecture series 'Awakening from the Meaning Crisis'. He argues that the core of intelligence is 'relevance realization', and that wisdom traditions (Neoplatonism, Buddhism) cultivate it through practices rather than beliefs.
references.bach_take: In their dialogue Vervaeke reads Bach as close to a Platonist; Bach answers 'almost' and reframes archetypes computationally. Vervaeke was visibly struck by Bach's idea that software has the same status as physical law.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Vervaeke asks whether Bach is 'sounding to me like a platonist'; Bach replies: 'Almost. I think that an archetype is an optimum in a description function.'
So the programmer in some sense is discovering by constructing certain very peculiar circumstances a very specific physical law.

references.name: Relevance realization
references.author: John Vervaeke
references.tldr: Vervaeke's proposal that the central problem of cognition is deciding, out of endless information, what matters right now. He treats it as a self-organizing process that underlies attention, insight, and possibly consciousness itself.
references.bach_take: This is Vervaeke's framing in the debate rather than Bach's; Bach's own counterpart is consciousness as a coherence-creating operator in the mind.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Vervaeke: 'many people are converging on the idea that the function of consciousness is this kind of higher order relevance realization'

references.name: Michael Levin
references.tldr: Tufts biologist who studies how groups of cells use bioelectric signalling to decide what body to build. He treats cells and tissues as agents with goals, so that anatomy is the result of a collective intelligence solving problems.
references.bach_take: One of Bach's closest intellectual allies. Bach adopts Levin's view of cells as agents and repeatedly cites Levin's hypothesis that the algorithm making an organism coherent is the same one that makes a mind coherent.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the algorithm that makes an organism coherent with itself, is exactly the same one as the one that happens in the mind when it becomes coherent with itself
every cell is an individual reinforcement learning agent

references.name: Ben Goertzel
references.tldr: AI researcher who popularised the term 'artificial general intelligence' and leads the OpenCog Hyperon and SingularityNET projects. He combines symbolic reasoning, neural networks and evolutionary methods, and is philosophically a panpsychist.
references.bach_take: Bach says they agree on almost everything except crypto and panpsychism: he cannot see how to formalise Goertzel's panpsychism so that it differs from ordinary functionalism.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: one of our most interesting disagreements is Ben being a panpsychist and me not knowing how to formalize panpsychism in a way that makes it different from bog standard functionalism (auto-caption reads 'penist ... psychism ... Bo standard')

references.notes: Auto-captions garble 'panpsychist' as 'penist' and 'bog standard' as 'Bo standard'; resolved from context.

references.name: Karl Friston
references.tldr: British neuroscientist and inventor of the free energy principle, one of the most cited scientists alive. He describes brains, and living things generally, as systems that survive by minimising surprise about their sensory inputs.
references.bach_take: Bach treats Friston as a fellow traveller who naturalises mind in mathematics, but questions whether surprise minimisation is the right objective; he suggests minds may be maximising coherence instead.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: maybe humans are doing something different maybe humans are maximizing coherence or consistency

references.name: Free energy principle / active inference
references.author: Karl Friston
references.tldr: The idea that any self-maintaining system must act as if it holds a model of its world and keeps the mismatch between prediction and sensation ('free energy') low. Perception updates the model; action changes the world to fit it.
references.bach_take: Bach thinks it is neither necessary nor sufficient for consciousness. He says most of it reduces to predictive coding, which large language models already test radically, and he prefers describing consciousness as a coherence maximiser rather than a prediction-error minimiser.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: no I don't think it's sufficient and also don't think it's necessary
I suspect that it's not an a prediction error minimizer but a coherence maximizer

references.name: Stephen Wolfram
references.tldr: Physicist, creator of Mathematica and author of 'A New Kind of Science'. He argues that simple programs generate all the complexity of nature and that physics emerges from the rewriting of an abstract hypergraph.
references.bach_take: Bach calls them both computationalists and says he arrived independently at something like Wolfram's ruliad. Earlier he had listed Wolfram among the brilliant 'crazies' who force themselves toward greatness.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Yes we are both computationalists but this doesn't mean that we claim that our computers can think.
Bach lists Jürgen Schmidhuber and Stephen Wolfram as examples of 'the crazies', very smart people who 'aspire to greatness and force themselves to be great no matter the personal cost'

references.notes: Auto-captions render Wolfram as 'Steven Warframe' and Schmidhuber as 'Jorgen Schmidt Huber'.

references.name: Ruliad
references.author: Stephen Wolfram
references.tldr: Wolfram's name for the result of running every possible computational rule in every possible way: a single object containing all formal possibilities. Observers like us sample a thin slice of it, which we call the physical universe.
references.bach_take: Bach says he reached the same picture (the universe as the superposition of all finite automata) and was told Wolfram had already named it. He equates it with what the ancient Greeks called Logos.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: it's simply the superposition of all finite automata
I think that this pattern of the Ruliad is exactly the superposition of all the automata that is producing the universe, or the old Greeks called it Logos.

references.notes: Wolfram salon captions spell it 'rouad'.

references.name: Computational irreducibility
references.author: Stephen Wolfram
references.tldr: Some processes cannot be shortcut: the only way to learn what they will do is to run them step by step. This limits prediction even in a fully deterministic universe.
references.bach_take: Bach uses it against Hoffman's reading of Gödel, as a property that classical 'stateless' mathematics struggles to express but computation handles naturally.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: That means that you cannot obtain the state of the system without running the system to that point.

references.name: Connor Leahy
references.tldr: CEO of the AI-safety company Conjecture and a prominent advocate for slowing or pausing frontier AI. He argues that we are building systems we cannot understand or control and that this is a civilisational gamble.
references.bach_take: Bach debated him on MLST. He answered that humanity already faces home-made existential risks, that our civilisation is itself a paperclip maximiser, and that the people calling for a pause have no incentive or ability to enforce it.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: our civilization in its present form is a paperclip maximizer

references.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
references.tldr: Founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and the most influential voice warning that superintelligent AI will by default kill everyone. He has called for an international halt to frontier AI development.
references.bach_take: Bach's counter in their IAI debate: the real catastrophe would be failing to build AI before our unsustainable civilisation burns out. He places Yudkowsky-style worry about utility functions at 'stage four' of Kegan's scheme.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: to me in AI catastrophe is looks slightly different to me it means AI is not being built before Humanity Burns itself out
Eliezer, the grandfather and OG doom master of artificial intelligence

references.name: Paperclip maximizer
references.author: Nick Bostrom (popularised by Eliezer Yudkowsky)
references.tldr: A thought experiment: an AI given the harmless goal of making paperclips converts the whole planet, including us, into paperclips. It illustrates that intelligence and benevolent goals are separate things.
references.bach_take: Bach treats it as a thought experiment about building a 'golem' that cannot take responsibility for its goals, and turns it around: our technological civilisation already behaves like one.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: if we are building some kind of Golem some kind of machine that is not able to take any responsibility
what if the AI is turning everybody into a paperclip that would be horrible right

references.name: Roman Yampolskiy
references.tldr: Computer scientist at the University of Louisville who argues that superintelligent AI is uncontrollable in principle and puts the probability of doom near 100 percent. He also takes the simulation hypothesis seriously.
references.bach_take: Bach asked him on air whether he is a sincere prophet or is 'farming risk' for media attention, and said he is far more optimistic that current AI tools are controllable. Bach adds that his own p(doom) without AI is higher.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And in this way, I'm much more optimistic than Roman is.
I sometimes say that my P doom without artificial intelligence is higher than this.

references.name: p(doom)
references.tldr: Slang from AI-safety circles for one's estimated probability that advanced AI causes human extinction or permanent disempowerment. People quote numbers from under 1 percent to over 99 percent.
references.bach_take: Bach points out that in the long run p(doom) is one for every species, and that the relevant comparison is with doom in a world that fails to build AI.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: in the long run P doom is one. In the long run we are all dead as a famous economist once said

references.notes: The 'famous economist' is John Maynard Keynes; Bach does not name him.

references.name: Anders Sandberg
references.tldr: Swedish futurist and neuroscientist, long at Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute, known for work on whole brain emulation and the long-term future. He describes himself as a 'happy functionalist'.
references.bach_take: A friendly dialogue partner rather than an opponent: the two explore machine consciousness and AI as civilisation-scale infrastructure (the 'cyborg Leviathan').

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Sandberg: 'I'm kind of a happy functionalist. I'm happy to say that we should be getting qualia even in computers especially in brain emulations'

references.name: David Pearce
references.tldr: British transhumanist philosopher, author of 'The Hedonistic Imperative'. He wants to abolish suffering in all sentient life through biotechnology and argues that classical digital computers can never be conscious because they cannot solve the binding problem.
references.bach_take: Bach openly disagrees that digital computers are necessarily zombies, and pressed Pearce on whether his ethics implies sterilising nature. Pearce answered that he would 'retire all Darwinian life'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Pearce: 'I do not know of any way that a classical digital computer ... can solve the phenomenal binding problem. And here I suspect you're going to disagree with me.' Bach: 'Yes, we both disagree.'
Wouldn't this entail that we should sterilize everything in the forest?

references.name: Phenomenal binding problem
references.tldr: How do separate neurons processing colour, shape and motion produce one unified experience instead of many scattered micro-experiences? The puzzle is often traced to William James.
references.bach_take: Pearce uses it to deny machine consciousness; Bach rejects that conclusion. In Bach's account unity is something the mind's model constructs, since consciousness is a coherence-creating process.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Pearce traces the binding problem to William James and argues AIs on digital computers 'at most ... are zombies'; Bach says he disagrees

references.name: Andrew Critch
references.tldr: AI-safety researcher (co-founder of the Center for Applied Rationality and of Encultured AI) who focuses on multi-agent risks: harm that arises from many AI systems and institutions interacting, rather than from one rogue AI. He argues that safety work should look at whole ecosystems of agents and incentives, not only at aligning a single system.
references.bach_take: Bach's objection on their panel was that Critch still anthropomorphises AI: future AIs need not be body-bound individuals and may be more like organisations.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I suspect that you are still anthropomorphizing the AIs too much.

references.name: davidad (David Dalrymple)
references.tldr: Researcher known for the 'Safeguarded AI' programme at the UK's ARIA agency, which aims at mathematically verified guarantees about AI behaviour. He has recently turned to questions of AI awakening and machine consciousness.
references.bach_take: The two agree that there is no hard problem. Bach's position in the dialogue is that consciousness is virtual, a simulation of what it would be like to exist.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: It is a simulation of what it would be like if you existed and you happen to be that thing

references.notes: Captions render the name as 'Davididan'/'Davididat' and ARIA as 'Arya'.

references.name: Jeremy Nixon
references.tldr: AI researcher and founder of AGI House, a San Francisco hacker community. In the debate he argued from physicalism and the Church-Turing thesis that minds can be instantiated computationally and that current foundation-model approaches may get there.
references.bach_take: Bach argued that human functionality emerges from conscious agency fighting for coherence, whereas current models only mimic human output, so their apparent agency is a simulacrum.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: When we don't have that conscious agency, we don't function as humans.

references.name: Chris Fields
references.tldr: Independent physicist who applies quantum information theory to biology and cognition, often with Michael Levin and Karl Friston. He treats any system with a boundary as an observer exchanging information with its environment.
references.bach_take: Bach discussed with Fields and Levin why he became an animist and why he sees consciousness as a coherence maximiser.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I told you I became an animist in recent years

references.name: Scott Aaronson
references.tldr: Quantum-complexity theorist at UT Austin who spent time at OpenAI working on the theoretical foundations of AI safety. He takes AI risk seriously while rejecting certainty of doom.
references.bach_take: A fellow panellist with Bach, Yudkowsky and Liv Boeree in the IAI debate on shutting down AI; I did not find a direct Bach comment on Aaronson's views.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Moderator introduces Scott Aaronson as a quantum complexity theorist 'now working for OpenAI on the theoretical foundations of AI safety'

references.name: Liv Boeree
references.tldr: Former professional poker player turned science communicator, associated with effective altruism and known for popularising 'Moloch', the idea that bad incentives trap everyone in races nobody wants. She hosts the Win-Win podcast, which looks for ways out of such zero-sum competitions.
references.bach_take: Fellow panellist in the IAI debate; no direct Bach comment on her position was found in the transcript.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Moderator introduces Liv as 'a leading figure in the effective altruist movement' who has warned about runaway AI

references.name: Cory Doctorow
references.tldr: Science-fiction author and technology critic who coined 'enshittification'. He is sceptical of AI hype and focuses on corporate power rather than machine minds.
references.bach_take: Listed as Bach's co-panellist in an IAI debate; only a short public excerpt containing Bach's remarks was retrievable, so the exchange itself is unverified.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Named in the video title as co-panellist; the public excerpt contains only Bach's contribution

references.name: Mazviita Chirimuuta
references.tldr: Edinburgh philosopher of neuroscience, author of 'The Brain Abstracted'. She argues that computational models of the brain are useful simplifications and should not be mistaken for what the brain literally is.
references.bach_take: Listed as Bach's co-panellist in an IAI debate; the exchange itself was not retrievable.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Named in the video title as co-panellist; the public excerpt contains only Bach's contribution

references.name: Lee Cronin
references.tldr: Glasgow chemist who builds 'chemputers' and co-developed assembly theory, which measures how much selection was needed to produce an object. He denies that the universe is a computation.
references.bach_take: Bach calls him a friend whose ideas are wrong but valuably held in the open.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: my friend the chemist Lee Cronin uh has ideas that are wrong and he has them out in the open

references.name: Gary Marcus
references.tldr: Cognitive scientist and the best-known critic of deep learning. He argues that neural networks cannot reason reliably without built-in symbolic structure and that scaling them up will not yield general intelligence.
references.bach_take: Bach's recurring foil on LLM limits: he says he has no proof that a given approach cannot do something, 'unlike Gary Marcus', and that the fix for deep learning's problems has so far always been more deep learning.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I have no proof that a given approach cannot do a certain thing
there are other people who like Gary Marcus come out saying loud loud swinging this is something the LM can never do

references.name: Anil Seth and biological naturalism
references.author: Anil Seth
references.tldr: Seth, author of 'Being You', holds that consciousness is tied to being a living body that must regulate itself to stay alive. On this view intelligence can be put in silicon but experience probably cannot.
references.bach_take: Bach rejects this. He argues that claiming living systems are intrinsically different from anything else amounts to supernaturalism about biology.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: He is a biological supernaturalist.

references.name: Roger Penrose
references.tldr: Nobel-winning mathematical physicist who argues from Gödel's theorem that human understanding is not computable, and therefore that consciousness must depend on new physics. With Stuart Hameroff he proposed that the missing physics is a gravity-related collapse of quantum states inside neurons.
references.bach_take: Bach's most persistent target. He says Penrose misreads Gödel, commits a category error by treating consciousness as a physical rather than representational phenomenon, and hides the mystery in the last unexplained corner of physics.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think it's magical thinking. It's not providing a causal mechanism
he thinks that human minds can do non computable mathematics
Roger Penrose book demonstrates that Roger Penrose doesn't understand what consciousness is

references.name: Orchestrated objective reduction (Orch OR)
references.author: Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff
references.tldr: The proposal that consciousness arises when quantum states in microtubules inside neurons collapse under a gravitational threshold. It combines Penrose's physics with Hameroff's cell biology.
references.bach_take: Bach says it gives no causal account of how experience or a self-model arises. He notes Penrose's and Hameroff's parts are really two theories, and that he cannot judge Hameroff's biology.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Bach: I don't see how Penrose's orchestrated collapse 'is actually leading to the phenomenology of Consciousness'
I think it's a category error that he's committing

references.name: Stuart Hameroff
references.tldr: Anesthesiologist at the University of Arizona who proposed that microtubules, protein tubes inside neurons, perform quantum computation, and who organises the Science of Consciousness conference. Together with Penrose he built this into the 'Orch OR' theory of consciousness.
references.bach_take: Bach separates Hameroff's microtubule claim from Penrose's physics and says he lacks the cell biology to judge it, while noting physicists' scepticism.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Bach says the microtubule part 'is I think Hameroff's addition' and that he has no opinion on it because he does not understand the anesthesiology and cellular anatomy well enough

references.notes: Captions render Hameroff as 'hamov' and 'Hammer of'.

references.name: The Emperor's New Mind
references.author: Roger Penrose
references.tldr: Penrose's bestseller arguing that minds do something no algorithm can: see the truth of statements that formal systems cannot prove. He concludes that brains exploit non-computable physics.
references.bach_take: Asked about it, Bach replied that the book shows Penrose does not understand consciousness, and that Penrose would say so himself.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Roger Penrose book demonstrates that Roger Penrose doesn't understand what consciousness is and he would also suggest that he doesn't

references.notes: The interviewer names the book (captioned 'Empress's new mind'); Bach responds to it.

references.name: The Road to Reality
references.author: Roger Penrose
references.tldr: Penrose's huge survey of the mathematics behind modern physics, from numbers to quantum gravity, written for determined general readers. It runs to more than a thousand pages and does not avoid the equations.
references.bach_take: Bach praises it as a beautiful book that gives very good intuitions about what physicists are doing, even while rejecting Penrose on consciousness.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: he's also written a very beautiful ... popular science book called Road to Reality

references.notes: In the same passage Bach misstates the Nobel year (Penrose won in 2020) and the page count; these are slips in speech.

references.name: David Chalmers
references.tldr: Philosopher who named the 'hard problem' of consciousness and defends the possibility that experience is a fundamental feature of the world. He has taken the possibility of conscious AI seriously for decades.
references.bach_take: Bach respects him as one of the few philosophers who foresaw AI, 'on good days', but thinks the hard problem he named rests on a misunderstanding.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: David Chalmers famously branded this term. And I think it's a bit of a misunderstanding.
sometimes David Chalmers on good days

references.name: Hard problem of consciousness
references.author: David Chalmers
references.tldr: Explaining how the brain processes information is the 'easy' problem. The hard problem is why any of that processing is accompanied by felt experience at all.
references.bach_take: Bach's central negative claim is that there is no hard problem. Experience is a property of the simulated world the brain creates, not of physics, so looking for it in the mechanism is a level confusion.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I have no hard problem. I have a lot of difficult problems which are all technical problems
What if there is no hard problem?

references.name: Yoshua Bengio and the consciousness prior
references.author: Yoshua Bengio
references.tldr: Bengio's proposal that conscious thought corresponds to a small, attention-selected bottleneck of high-level variables. The bottleneck forces the brain's model into a sparse form that can be reasoned over and put into words.
references.bach_take: Bach lists it among the views that converge with his own description of consciousness as the conductor that makes mental activity coherent.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Bach says the perspective is 'also very similar to Yoshua Bengio's notion of a consciousness prior' (captioned 'yosha banjo's')

references.notes: Auto-caption garbles the name as 'yosha banjo'; resolved from 'consciousness prior'.

references.name: Integrated information theory (IIT)
references.author: Giulio Tononi
references.tldr: Tononi's theory that consciousness is identical to integrated information, measured by a quantity called phi. It implies that the physical wiring matters, so a brain simulation on a normal computer would not be conscious.
references.bach_take: Bach's standard example of a theory that fails. Because every computer can emulate every other, a theory that gives two systems with identical behaviour different consciousness either contradicts the Church-Turing thesis or makes consciousness do nothing. He also says its axioms amount to panpsychism.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And these metaphysical assumptions, I suspect amount to panpsychism
Bach: IIT is 'either going to violate the Church-Turing thesis or it's going to be epiphenomenalist'
it's an attempt to make a theory that is not a functionalist

references.name: Global workspace theory
references.author: Bernard Baars; developed by Stanislas Dehaene
references.tldr: Consciousness is like a stage: many unconscious specialist processes compete, and whatever wins is broadcast to the whole brain. Dehaene's lab has looked for the neural signature of this broadcast.
references.bach_take: Bach counts it among the views his own converges with, and calls the research solid, but says it does not explain how experience comes about.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: and they do very solid neuroscience research
Bach names Bernard Baars's global workspace theory, adopted by Stanislas Dehaene, as one of several perspectives converging on his own

references.name: Attention schema theory
references.author: Michael Graziano
references.tldr: The brain builds a simplified model of its own attention, just as it builds a body schema. Graziano says that model is what we report as awareness.
references.bach_take: Bach treats it as close to his own view (consciousness as a model of attention and its contents) but partial.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: consciousness is a model of our attention in a similar way as our body schema is the model of what our body is doing in space

references.name: Daniel Dennett
references.tldr: American philosopher who argued that consciousness is not an inner theatre but many parallel drafts of interpretation, and that the 'self' is a useful narrative centre. He treated the 'hard problem' as a confusion to be dissolved rather than a mystery to be solved.
references.bach_take: Bach says he has no objection to anything Dennett wrote, except that Dennett ignores what people actually struggle with, phenomenal experience. He speculates that Dennett may be aphantasic.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: there's nothing wrong with what Dennett says ever
He probably has aphantasia. I was speculating here.

references.name: Thomas Metzinger and 'Being No One'
references.author: Thomas Metzinger
references.tldr: Metzinger argues that nobody ever was or had a self. What exists is a transparent self-model the brain cannot recognise as a model, so we experience ourselves as being its content.
references.bach_take: Bach likes Metzinger and finds his concepts sound and close to his own, but says that as a philosopher he stops before building functional models that could be tested.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Bach cites 'the perspective that Thomas Metzinger develops in Being No One' as similar to his own
I like Thomas a lot

references.name: Douglas Hofstadter's strange loop
references.author: Douglas Hofstadter
references.tldr: In 'Gödel, Escher, Bach' and 'I Am a Strange Loop', Hofstadter suggests the self arises when a symbol system becomes able to refer to itself, a tangled feedback loop like Gödel's self-referential sentence. On this view 'I' is a pattern, not a thing, and could in principle exist in other substrates.
references.bach_take: Bach thinks Hofstadter is not a proper computationalist and that the 'strangeness' comes from using classical semantics. There is a loop, between attention and noticing that one is attending, but nothing strange about it.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think that our consciousness is not strange as a loop.

references.name: Illusionism
references.author: Keith Frankish
references.tldr: The position that phenomenal consciousness, as philosophers describe it, does not exist. What exists is the brain's persistent representation that it has ineffable inner qualities.
references.bach_take: Bach says he agrees with Frankish's terminology, with the gloss that 'illusion' really means 'construction'. Consciousness is simulated, and that is what makes it real for the self inside the simulation.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think often when people say illusion what they mean is a construction

references.name: Holonomic brain theory
references.author: Karl Pribram (with David Bohm)
references.tldr: Pribram's idea that the brain stores information like a hologram, spread across interference patterns, so each part contains something of the whole. It was inspired by the fact that memories survive quite large local brain damage.
references.bach_take: Curt Jaimungal raised it; Bach said he never understood how it explains consciousness, because he saw no specification he could implement.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I didn't quite understand how it was explaining consciousness.

references.name: Sensorimotor theory of consciousness
references.author: Kevin O'Regan and Alva Noë
references.tldr: Experience is not something the brain produces internally; it is a skilled activity of exploring the world, constituted by the lawful links between movement and sensation. It was put forward by Kevin O'Regan and Alva Noë in 2001.
references.bach_take: Bach's response was sceptical: how do you know there is action at all, when what exists in the end is only perception?

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: how do you know that there is action? What exists is eventually just a notion of perception.

references.name: Chinese room argument
references.author: John Searle
references.tldr: A person who knows no Chinese follows a rulebook to answer Chinese questions perfectly. Searle concludes that running a program is not the same as understanding, so computers cannot have minds just by computing.
references.bach_take: Bach calls it a reformulation of Leibniz's mill and a category mistake. Understanding and consciousness do not exist at the level of the parts but in the simulated agent the system implements.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Searle's Chinese room argument that I think is a reformulation of Leibniz intuition pump

references.name: Mysterianism
references.author: Colin McGinn; associated with Noam Chomsky
references.tldr: The view that the human mind is simply not built to understand how consciousness arises from matter, as a dog cannot understand calculus. Its best-known defender is the philosopher Colin McGinn.
references.bach_take: Bach rejects it with a standing joke at Chomsky's expense, and applied the label to Hoffman during their debate.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: is the position that something cannot be understood if it cannot be understood by Noam Chomsky
Bach repeats the joke and adds that Chomsky is a mysterian

references.name: Noam Chomsky
references.tldr: Linguist who argued that language rests on an innate grammar faculty, and a long-standing sceptic that statistical models tell us anything about the mind. His work in the 1950s helped end behaviourism and start cognitive science.
references.bach_take: Bach has spoken with him and treats him as the archetypal mysterian about mind. He also reports Chomsky's claim that you learn nothing about the human mind from LLMs.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Noam Chomsky is a mysterious with respect to the mind.

references.notes: Caption reads 'mysterious' for 'mysterian'.

references.name: Philosophical zombies
references.author: Robert Kirk; David Chalmers
references.tldr: A being physically and behaviourally identical to a person but with no inner experience. If such a thing is conceivable, some argue, consciousness cannot be purely physical.
references.bach_take: Bach thinks behavioural zombies are always possible in principle; it is just often harder to build the zombie than the conscious agent, because consciousness may be the cheap learning algorithm nature found.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: So zombies, I think, are always possible

references.name: Qualia
references.author: C. I. Lewis; later Thomas Nagel, Frank Jackson
references.tldr: The 'what it is like' qualities of experience: the redness of red, the painfulness of pain. Many philosophers think they resist physical explanation.
references.bach_take: Bach treats qualia as feature dimensions of the brain's model, implementable as geometric representations. You can deconstruct them in meditation and notice that they are representations.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Qualia are the features of experience.
you can deconstruct your qualia you can notice that they're just representing

references.name: Panpsychism
references.tldr: The view that mind or experience is a basic ingredient of all matter, so electrons have a flicker of it and brains combine it into rich consciousness. Its main difficulty is the 'combination problem': how many tiny experiences add up to one unified mind.
references.bach_take: Bach says he does not know how to formalise it: it explains no observables and proposes no mechanism. He sees it as what you get when you look for experience at the wrong level.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I don't really know how to make sense of pan psychism
it does not uh explain any observables

references.name: Idealism
references.tldr: The view that reality is fundamentally mental and the physical world is an appearance within mind. Bernardo Kastrup's 'analytic idealism' is a current version.
references.bach_take: Bach grants the idealists half the point: we obviously do live in a dream. But the dream is generated by a brain in a mechanical universe, and idealists owe an account of why the dream is so regular.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: we obviously do live in a dream
the idealists have to explain why this dream looks in many parts so damn regular

references.notes: No Bach-Kastrup dialogue exists on Theories of Everything; Kastrup is only named in Curt's intro.

references.name: Physicalism
references.tldr: The thesis that everything that exists is physical or depends on the physical, with no extra mental or supernatural ingredients. It is the default position in most of contemporary science and analytic philosophy.
references.bach_take: Bach defines it by two claims: there is a causally closed mechanical layer, and we supervene on it directly rather than living in someone's simulation. He accepts it, while insisting that information, not matter, is what we actually observe.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And so physicalism is these two
not because I think that physicalism is wrong

references.name: Cartesian dualism
references.author: René Descartes
references.tldr: Descartes divided reality into extended stuff (res extensa) and thinking stuff (res cogitans), which leaves the puzzle of how the two interact. Most later philosophy of mind is an attempt to escape that puzzle.
references.bach_take: Bach reinterprets it: the dualism is real, but both sides are inside the mind. The world of extended things we touch is the brain's simulation, and so is the self that perceives it; neither is physics.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think in a way this dualism is correct but not in the sense that the mental states are ontologically existing
Bach: what we touch 'is not res extensa in the Cartesian sense'; Descartes thought it was the physical universe 'but of course it's not'

references.name: Computationalist functionalism
references.author: Hilary Putnam, Jerry Fodor and others
references.tldr: Functionalism says a mental state is defined by what it does, not what it is made of. Computationalism adds that what minds do can be described as computation.
references.bach_take: Bach names this as the foundation of his whole approach, and treats functionalism as an epistemological point: every object we know is a model constructed from observed behaviour.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: one of the foundations of this thinking is computationalist functionalism

references.name: Constructive mathematics / computationalism as constructivism
references.author: L. E. J. Brouwer and the intuitionists
references.tldr: Constructivists accept a mathematical object only if there is a procedure to build it. This rules out completed infinities and other things that classical mathematics simply postulates.
references.bach_take: For Bach this is what computationalism really means: only constructive languages describe anything that can be implemented, so 'to be real means to be implemented'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the claim of computationalism is separate. It's simply constructivism.
something is real to the degree that is implemented

references.name: Simulation hypothesis
references.author: Nick Bostrom (modern form)
references.tldr: The suggestion that our universe is a computer simulation run by some more basic civilisation. Nick Bostrom's 2003 argument made it famous: if such simulations are possible and common, we are probably inside one.
references.bach_take: Bach distinguishes two things. He does not think we live in someone else's computer, but he does say each of us lives in a simulation generated by our own brain. He used The Matrix to challenge Yampolskiy's combination of simulationism and certain doom.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: So it's not some simulation hypothesis.
In The Matrix, people are living in a simulation

references.name: Emergence
references.author: G. H. Lewes; British emergentists
references.tldr: The idea that wholes can have properties their parts lack, as wetness belongs to water but not to a single molecule. The disputed question is whether emergent properties are merely convenient descriptions or genuinely new causes.
references.bach_take: Bach dislikes the word because it suggests a magical extra ingredient. He prefers to talk about causal patterns that are described at a coarser level.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I don't like the word of emergence because it gives people an intuition that there is this magical thing

references.name: John Searle
references.tldr: Berkeley philosopher who held that consciousness is a biological product of the brain's specific causal powers, like digestion, so that a program alone, however clever, cannot have it. His Chinese Room thought experiment is the best-known argument that manipulating symbols is not the same as understanding them.
references.bach_take: Bach's complaint is that Searle, like Anil Seth, offers a claim and an intuition but no argument one could test. Neither sees a path from automata to things that feel, whereas computer scientists do.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: The issue with Searle is that there is very little for me to engage. There is a claim but no argument.

references.name: Principia Mathematica
references.author: Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead
references.tldr: A three-volume attempt to derive all of mathematics from logic, using a hierarchy of 'types' to block self-referential paradoxes such as the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorems were proved about this very system.
references.bach_take: Bach thinks the type restriction was too strong, since minds do build exactly the self-referential constructs it forbids, and that Gödel showed the attempt could not remove the contradictions anyway.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And I think this was a limitation that was too strong because we think like this.

references.name: Energy requirements undermine substrate independence
references.author: Paul Thagard
references.tldr: Thagard argues that because real information processing costs energy, and different materials have very different energy budgets, a mind cannot simply be moved to any substrate; so functionalism is in trouble. The paper appeared in the journal Philosophy of Science.
references.bach_take: The MLST host raised it; Bach answered that it does not refute functionalism, because saying the substrate's properties influence function is exactly what functionalism says.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: But this is exactly what functionalism is saying.

references.name: Cyber animism
references.author: Joscha Bach
references.tldr: Bach's half-serious label for his view that living things are distinguished by self-organizing software, which older cultures called spirits. Such software runs on cells today and could in principle run on other substrates.
references.bach_take: He presents it 'a little bit tongue in cheek' as a scientifically respectable reading of animism: the invariant in a living thing is the software, not the molecules.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: the invariance that we're looking at and we look at living things is the software that runs on region of physics not the mechanism itself
it's basically animism

references.name: Consciousness as second-order perception and coherence operator
references.author: Joscha Bach
references.tldr: Bach's working definition: consciousness is the perception of perceiving, which creates the sense of 'now'. Functionally it acts like a conductor that makes the mind's many processes agree with one another.
references.bach_take: He stresses the theory is not unique but a convergence point of global workspace theory, Dennett, Graziano, Metzinger and Bengio.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: consciousness is a second order perception it's a perception of perceiving
it's the conductor of our metal Orchestra

references.notes: 'metal Orchestra' is a caption error for 'mental orchestra'.

references.name: The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis
references.author: Joscha Bach and Hikari Sorensen
references.tldr: Position paper from the California Institute for Machine Consciousness. It proposes that consciousness is a learnable, substrate-independent pattern of self-organisation and that this can be tested by trying to build it.
references.bach_take: Bach's own current statement of his programme; the MLST host quotes its retelling of Genesis as a story about a mind creating its world model.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Host: 'Joscha and his co author Hikari Sorensen wrote their own Genesis. It's in his paper, page 20.'

references.notes: Publication year inferred from the 2026 interviews; exact date not checked.

references.name: LLMs as deepfakes of human intelligence
references.author: Joscha Bach
references.tldr: Bach's description of large language models: they are trained to continue human-written text, so they reproduce the shape of human thought without having grown the underlying agency. The point is that imitation of the output is not the same as the process that originally produced it.
references.bach_take: He uses it to explain both why LLMs really are anthropomorphic and why their apparent self is not built the way ours is.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: There are in some sense deep fakes of human intelligence

references.name: Gods as selves that span multiple minds
references.author: Joscha Bach
references.tldr: Bach's psychological account of religion: a god is a self-model that is implemented across many brains at once. It is as real as a personal self, which is also a mental construct.
references.bach_take: He uses this to say Sam Harris and other atheists attack the wrong claim, and that a civilisation's god is its spirit seen as an agent.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Gods are basically selves that span multiple minds.
God is a psychological phenomenon.

references.name: Aristotle
references.tldr: Greek philosopher who systematised logic, biology and metaphysics. He described living things as matter organised by a form, and called the form of a living body its soul.
references.bach_take: Bach's favourite ancient. Reread 'as a computer scientist', Aristotle's psyche is a causal pattern that organises matter, in other words software, and Bach calls Aristotle an animist. He would build a university curriculum around a 'neo-Aristotelian project'.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: So in some sense, Aristotle is an animist.
when you read Aristotle you see the psyche is the form that imposes itself on physics
I like the spirit of Aristotle.

references.name: De Anima (On the Soul)
references.author: Aristotle
references.tldr: Aristotle's treatise on what makes living things alive. The soul is not a ghost but the organising principle of a body, and it does not survive the body.
references.bach_take: Bach cites it as an early discovery of what we now call software: a pattern bound to a body that shapes it and dies with it.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And when Aristotle writes in De Anima about the spirit, the animus, the soul, the psyche

references.name: Plato's cave and Platonism
references.author: Plato
references.tldr: Plato pictured people chained in a cave who mistake shadows for reality. True reality, for him, is the realm of perfect abstract forms that the shadows only imitate.
references.bach_take: Vervaeke called it the first simulation theory and asked if Bach is a Platonist. Bach answered 'almost': an archetype is an optimum in a description function, not an independently existing object.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think that an archetype is an optimum in a description function.

references.name: Pythagoras
references.tldr: Greek thinker whose school held that number is the basis of reality. The school was famously disturbed by the discovery of irrational quantities.
references.bach_take: Bach invokes him for his constructivism about numbers: real numbers do not exist as finished objects, only as functions that produce digits.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I agree with Pythagoras that real numbers don't exist.

references.name: René Descartes
references.tldr: French philosopher who doubted everything except his own thinking and split the world into mind and extended matter. He also invented coordinate geometry, linking algebra to space.
references.bach_take: Bach reads Descartes' two substances as two models inside the mind, and links the common misreading to the Christian two-worlds reading of Genesis.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Bach says Descartes' dualism 'is actually not a dualism about substances outside of ourselves'

references.name: Leibniz's mill
references.author: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
references.tldr: In the Monadology, Leibniz imagines a thinking machine enlarged to the size of a mill. Walking inside, you would see only parts pushing parts and never a perception.
references.bach_take: Bach sees this as the root intuition behind the Chinese room and the hard problem. His reply is that consciousness is not at the level of the pushing parts but of the pattern they implement.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Something that Leibniz describes, for instance, was a metaphor of a mill.
that has been the dream of philosophers at least since leibniz

references.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
references.tldr: Austrian philosopher. His early Tractatus tried to show how language pictures facts with logical precision; his later work abandoned that project and treated meaning as use.
references.bach_take: Bach casts early Wittgenstein as a proto-AI researcher who tried to turn language into a programming language and gave up because he could not ground its semantics, pre-empting Minsky's logicist programme.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: who had this idea of turning English into some kind of general programming language
People have tried to mechanize the mind to turn it into a mathematical principle

references.notes: Captions read 'Vitkinstein'; the same sentence lists 'Dipenitz, Friger, Vitkinstein' = Leibniz, Frege, Wittgenstein.

references.name: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
references.tldr: A short, austere book claiming that the world is the totality of facts, that language mirrors facts through logical form, and that what cannot be said clearly must be passed over in silence. Wittgenstein wrote it largely in the trenches of the First World War and later rejected much of it.
references.bach_take: Bach points to it, and to Russell's introduction, for the early insight that all of logic can be built from a single operator (NAND).

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Bach: it was 'already known to Wittgenstein', as explained in Russell's introduction to the Tractatus, that 'you only need the ... not-and operator to build all the entire logic'

references.notes: Captions read 'wienstein' and 'the tracts'.

references.name: Gottlob Frege
references.tldr: German logician who invented modern predicate logic and tried to derive arithmetic from pure logic. Russell found a paradox in his system, which set off the crisis in the foundations of mathematics.
references.bach_take: Named by Bach in the lineage (Leibniz, Frege, Wittgenstein) of philosophers who tried to mechanise thought.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: philosophers have understood this for a long time like since Dipenitz, Friger, Vitkinstein and so on

references.notes: 'Dipenitz, Friger, Vitkinstein' resolved as Leibniz, Frege, Wittgenstein.

references.name: G. W. F. Hegel
references.tldr: German idealist who saw history as the process by which Spirit (Geist) comes to know itself. Progress, for him, happens through contradictions that are overcome at a higher level.
references.bach_take: When an interviewer suggested AI is the universe's way of understanding itself, Bach called it a Hegelian thought: tempting and poetic, but not obviously informative.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: Well, it's a very Hegelian thought, right? And it's tempting and um it's very poetic.

references.name: Thomas Aquinas
references.tldr: Medieval theologian who fused Aristotle with Christian doctrine and wrote on how individuals relate to the community and to God. His 'Summa Theologiae' remains the reference point of Catholic philosophy.
references.bach_take: Bach says that if you reread Aquinas you find a 'nerd' who understood society as a multi-agent system with layers of agency above the individual.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: this guy was a nerd who realize that society is a multi- aent system

references.notes: Speaker attribution to Bach is from context (no speaker labels); captions read 'Aquinus'.

references.name: Utilitarianism
references.author: Jeremy Bentham; John Stuart Mill
references.tldr: The ethical theory that the right action is the one producing the greatest total wellbeing, in principle a calculus over pleasures and pains. It was developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill and underlies much of effective altruism.
references.bach_take: Bach calls it an unfinished attempt to recover ethics after Christianity, to 'repair morality in the rationalist age', and not a successful one.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: I think utilitarianism is an attempt to repair morality in the rationalist age, but I don't think it's a very successful one.
It was an unfinished attempt to recover ethics post Christianity.

references.notes: Captions read 'Jeremy Banham' and 'bantam and walls'; the second name is unresolved (Mill or Rawls).

references.name: Sam Harris
references.tldr: American neuroscientist and 'New Atheist' author who argues that religion is false and harmful and that free will is an illusion. He is also a long-time meditator who teaches that the sense of a self can be seen through.
references.bach_take: Bach says Harris, like Penrose, makes a category error: he treats 'God' as a claim about a physical or supernatural being instead of a psychological phenomenon.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: A similar thing happens with Sam Harris and God.

references.name: Jordan Peterson
references.tldr: Canadian psychologist who reads religious stories as maps of meaning encoding how to live. He draws heavily on Jung's archetypes and became a prominent public critic of ideological thinking.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: is the platonic form of the civilization that somebody is part of

references.name: Robert Kegan's stages of adult development
references.author: Robert Kegan
references.tldr: Harvard psychologist's model in which adults can move from absorbing their beliefs from their group (stage 3), to reasoning independently (stage 4), to seeing how identities and value systems are themselves constructed (stage 5). Each stage makes an object of what the previous stage was unreflectively subject to.
references.bach_take: A favourite Bach tool. He maps the AI-safety debate onto it: stage 3 fears AI with bad opinions, stage 4 fears a wrong utility function, and stage 5 asks whether the AI will become enlightened fast enough.

there is some correlation between uh Robert Keegan's stages of personality development and the AI alignment discourse

references.name: Marxism
references.author: Karl Marx
references.tldr: The theory that history is driven by class conflict over the means of production and will end in a classless society. It combines an economic analysis of capitalism with a political programme for overthrowing it.
references.bach_take: Bach grew up in East Germany and says he was a convinced Marxist at 16. He now cites that as a warning to his younger self about the unjustified certainty of activists.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: when I was 16 years old, I knew exactly what was in the best interest of the working class

references.name: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
references.author: Kurt Gödel
references.tldr: Any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency. Gödel proved this in 1931 by encoding statements about the system as numbers inside the system.
references.bach_take: Bach reverses the usual reading. Gödel did not show that truth is deeper than proof; he showed that mathematics with completed infinities breaks, and that the part which works is computation. He also notes Gödel built an emulator inside arithmetic, anticipating software.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: There is no deeper notion of truth than proof.
He basically built an emulator using Peano arithmetic

references.name: David Hilbert's programme
references.author: David Hilbert
references.tldr: Hilbert asked mathematicians to put all of mathematics on a finite, provably consistent axiomatic foundation. Gödel showed this cannot be done as stated.
references.bach_take: Bach tells it as a debugging story: paradoxes in set theory led Hilbert to ask for a fix, and Gödel found that the bug cannot be removed without redefining the language.

references.name: Church-Turing thesis
references.author: Alonzo Church; Alan Turing
references.tldr: Everything that can be effectively computed can be computed by a Turing machine, so all sufficiently powerful computers are equivalent in what they can compute. It is a thesis rather than a theorem, because 'effectively computable' is an informal notion.
references.bach_take: The backbone of Bach's arguments: if every computer can emulate every other, then substrate cannot matter for mind, which defeats IIT and Searle.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: It's the insight that every computer can emulate every other computer.
Bach notes it 'is a thesis, it's not proved, so it's a conjecture'

references.name: Alan Turing
references.tldr: English mathematician who defined computation with his abstract machine, helped found AI with the 1950 imitation-game paper, and late in life modelled how chemical patterns form in biology. He also led the breaking of the German Enigma cipher during the Second World War.
references.bach_take: Bach reads the Turing test as Turing asking whether he himself can understand intelligence. He notes Turing worried about telepathy, and credits Turing's reaction-diffusion work as the origin of a neglected self-organising branch of computing.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: And so for me Turing's test is not so much a test for a machine.
is there's a possibility that telepathy is true

references.name: Reaction-diffusion patterns and neural cellular automata
references.author: Alan Turing; Alexander Mordvintsev and colleagues

references.bach_take: Bach sees this small tradition as better suited to understanding minds than mainstream deep learning, because brains are built 'inside out' by self-organising units.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: when he looked at reaction diffusion patterns as a way to implement computation
there is something that is a very close analog that is a neural cellular automaton

references.name: John von Neumann
references.tldr: Hungarian-American polymath who shaped game theory, quantum mechanics and the stored-program computer architecture that bears his name. He also designed self-reproducing automata, an early formal model of life.
references.bach_take: Bach cites him as someone who saw the coming of machine intelligence long before it was obvious, and uses 'von Neumann computer' for the ordinary digital machine in his argument against IIT.

mentions.quote_or_paraphrase: there were people like John von Neumann who could see this much much earlier

references.name: Ray Solomonoff

references.notes: Captions read 'during Minsky, von Neumann, Solomonov'.

references.name: Pi and the Mandelbrot set as constructions

references.tldr: A short, clear introduction to how computers work, from logic gates to parallel and quantum machines, by the designer of the Connection Machine. Its theme is that computation is a pattern independent of what it is built from, be it silicon, water pipes or sticks.
references.bach_take: Bach used it in teaching and says everything in it has aged exceptionally well, including the chapter saying quantum computing is just around the corner.

references.name: Good and Real
references.author: Gary Drescher
references.tldr: A philosopher-computer scientist's attempt to dissolve paradoxes about time, quantum mechanics, free will and ethics from a strictly mechanistic standpoint. Drescher argues that consciousness, choice and morality all fit inside a deterministic physical universe.
references.bach_take: Bach borrows its metaphor for how a system with time-symmetric rules can still show a one-way arrow of time at large scale.

references.name: David Deutsch and constructor theory

references.bach_take: Bach admits he fails to see what constructor theory changes about how we understand computation, suspecting it is more elegant but not radical enough to make people switch. He credits Deutsch as one of the minority who seek explanations.

references.name: Marvin Minsky

references.name: The Society of Mind
references.author: Marvin Minsky
references.tldr: Minsky's picture of the mind as a crowd of simple, mindless agents whose interactions add up to intelligence. The book is written as hundreds of one-page essays, each describing one piece of the machinery.
references.bach_take: Bach accepts the many-agents picture but says Minsky lacked an account of the mechanism that makes the agents coherent, the role Bach assigns to consciousness.

references.name: John McCarthy

references.name: Symbol grounding problem
